keyTerms.note: From the root for a foot sliding on wet or polished ground. It places the event in the category of losing footing rather than of planning a wrong, and the tradition keeps to that register.
A verb suggesting meeting something coming toward you and taking it up. Adam does not compose the words. They arrive, and his part is to receive them and use them.
An intensive form from the verb for turning back, the same verb used of the human being who repents. One root carries both movements, which is why the tradition speaks of a turning that is met.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A settled place and a stretch of time to enjoy it were exactly what a person in that world was working for. Nomadic families moved between grazing grounds and named the spot they stopped at differently from the road they travelled. Townspeople measured security in a house, a well and a grove that would still be there next year. Being granted a resting place and a limited term named the ordinary human situation precisely.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic of the second ayah uses one verbal root for both sides of the exchange. The human being turns back and God turns toward him, and the divine name that closes the sentence is built from that same root in its most intensive form. English needs two different words for the two movements, so the connection disappears in translation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The sequence puts the remedy inside the account of the fall rather than after it, and it gives the words to the one who needs them rather than requiring him to find them. That establishes something about the shape of return: it is offered before it is asked for. The passage also refuses to let the first human failure define the human being. The story does not end at the descent, and the last word in it is a name of mercy.

crossReferences.why: Preserves the prayer that commentators most often identify with the words received here.
Adds that after the turning came both choosing and guidance, continuing the account past this point.
Extends the same opening to everyone, telling those who wronged themselves not to despair.

studies.applyIt: If there is something you have been carrying without ever putting into words, borrow words rather than waiting to compose your own. Say a short established prayer of return tonight, exactly as it stands, even if it does not feel like yours yet. This passage has the words arriving first and the feeling following, which is the order most people actually find workable.

studies.title: A Way Back Given Immediately
studies.meaning: The instruction to go down is repeated from two ayat earlier, and commentators note that a repetition in the Quran normally carries something new. Here what is new is everything attached to it. The exile arrives with a provision already built in: guidance will come, and following it removes two things at once. The pair named covers the whole of a person's time, one word for dread of what is ahead and one for sorrow over what is behind. The following ayah states the other outcome with equal plainness.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the surah's account of the first human being and forming the bridge to the long address that follows. No occasion is reported. Classical commentators treat these two ayat as the hinge of the whole narrative, since everything the surah goes on to say about scripture, prophets and communities is an instance of the guidance promised here in general terms.

keyTerms.note: A plural command, though only two people have been in the scene. Commentators read the widening as taking in the whole line to come, which is why the promise attached to it is stated for everyone.
Indefinite in the Arabic: some guidance, any guidance, from Me. The form leaves the shape and the timing open while making the fact of it certain, which is the balance the sentence needs.
Sorrow over what has already happened, distinct from the fear named just before it, which looks forward. The two words together take in both directions of time and leave nothing between them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Expulsion was the heaviest sanction that world had. A man put out of his clan lost the protection that made ordinary life possible, and could be injured or killed with nobody obliged to answer for it. Readmission needed a mediator and a settlement. Being sent out with the terms of return stated in the same breath was not how any of that worked, and the audience would have heard the difference at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about having no fear and no grief becomes a fixed formula in the Quran, recurring in surah after surah for those under God's protection. This is its first appearance in the order of the text, and it arrives at the very moment humanity is sent out of the Garden, which is the least likely place for a formula of security to begin.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage arranges consequence and remedy in an order that matters. Nothing is withheld until the descent has been endured, and no interval is left between the loss and the offer. That says something specific about how the relationship is meant to run, namely that the initiative is not the human being's to take first. The alternative outcome is stated in the next ayah without softening, so the assurance is a genuine choice rather than a general reassurance.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the formula for the friends of God, with no fear upon them and no grief.
Gives the parallel telling, promising that whoever follows the guidance will neither stray nor be wretched.
Attaches the same assurance to those who say our Lord is God and then remain upright.

studies.applyIt: Write down one thing you are afraid of and one thing you regret, on the same piece of paper, in one line each. Notice that they point in opposite directions in time and that you have been carrying both at once. You do not need to solve either today. Seeing them side by side is what this ayah is arranged to let you do.

studies.title: Keep Yours And I Keep Mine
studies.meaning: The surah turns to a new audience and opens not with an argument but with a memory. Three things are asked in one line: recall what was given, complete what was pledged, and hold God in awe. The middle clause is the striking one, since it uses the same verb on both sides. The word is a merchant's term for paying a measure in full, and by using it of God as well the sentence casts the relationship as an account both parties settle rather than as a demand made in one direction.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and the beginning of the surah's long address to the Children of Israel. Medina had substantial and long-established Jewish communities with a scholarly tradition, palm groves and fortified quarters, and the early agreement of the city included them. The address that opens here is directed at neighbours with standing and a shared prophetic history, and commentators read the appeal to memory as resting on exactly that history.

keyTerms.note: A singular noun used for a whole history of provision. Commentators note the singular and read it as gathering many gifts into one continuous act rather than listing them as separate items.
The word a trader uses for completing a measure with nothing held back. It carries the image of a scale that must balance, and it appears on both sides of this sentence.
From a root joining fear to withdrawal and reverence. It names an alertness before something greater than oneself rather than fright, and Arabic uses the same root for a life given over to devotion.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Short measure was the classic market fraud and everyone had a view about it. Grain and dates were sold by volume in vessels a buyer could not easily check, and traders known for a full measure carried a reputation worth more than a season's margin. Agreements between clans worked the same way: what mattered was whether a party delivered the whole of what had been said aloud, in front of witnesses, at the time promised.
studies.didYouKnow: The address opened here does not close quickly. The surah keeps speaking to this audience, with only brief turns aside, for roughly eighty ayat, recalling a long sequence of episodes from their history. It is the most sustained address of its kind anywhere in the Quran, and it comes at the front of the longest surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Casting a covenant in the vocabulary of trade makes it mutual without making it equal. God is described as fulfilling an obligation, which is a remarkable thing for a scripture to say about an omnipotent party, and the tradition understands it as an obligation freely undertaken rather than one imposed from outside. The order of the clauses matters too. Memory comes first, since a pledge nobody remembers the reason for is not going to be kept.

crossReferences.why: Records the taking of the covenant itself, with the specific undertakings attached on both sides.
States the general principle of fulfilling God's covenant once entered into, and not breaking oaths after confirming them.
Ties gratitude to increase, connecting the remembering asked here to what follows from it.

studies.applyIt: Name three things you were given that you did nothing to earn, going back as far as childhood: a teacher, a language, a place to live. Say them out loud once. Then look at one commitment you made and have been half-keeping. The order in this ayah is deliberate, and remembering first tends to make the second part easier.

studies.title: Do Not Sell It Cheaply
studies.meaning: The new revelation is introduced as confirming what the audience already has, not as replacing it, and the participle used comes from the root for truthfulness. Then two warnings. The first is oddly specific: not do not reject it, but do not be the first to. Commentators read this as weight placed on precedent, since those who could recognise a thing set the terms for everyone watching. The second names a trade, and calls the price small without reference to its size.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, early in the surah's address to the Children of Israel. Commentators place these ayat in the years after the migration, when the community had settled among long-established neighbours who possessed scripture and scholarly standing. The tone is an appeal rather than a verdict, and the classical works read it as addressed to a moment of decision rather than as a description of a settled outcome.

keyTerms.note: From the root for truth in speech, which also gives the word for charity given from wealth. The participle presents the new revelation as certifying what came before rather than as competing with it.
The ordinary word for first in sequence. Its presence changes the warning entirely, making the issue one of who moves first and what follows from that rather than of the position itself.
A price, and an adjective calling it little. Commentators observe that the smallness is not a measure of the sum but of what it buys, so any worldly return would be described this way.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: There were no fixed prices in a seventh-century market. Every sale was struck by argument, and everybody knew the particular shame of a man who had let something valuable go cheap because he needed cash that week. Selling a she-camel before the season, or a stand of palms to cover a debt, was the sort of decision people remembered about a family for years. The vocabulary of a bad price carried all of that.
studies.didYouKnow: The word rendered as confirming shares its root with two very different Arabic words: the ordinary term for telling the truth, and the term for money given away from one's wealth. Lexicographers connect them through the idea of something proving genuine, whether a statement, a gift, or in this ayah a book measured against an earlier one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Presenting revelation as confirmation rather than replacement establishes a continuity that runs through the whole Quran, where the prophets form one line carrying one essential message. That has a consequence the ayah then draws: recognising something is not a neutral event, because whoever is positioned to recognise it carries more weight in what they do next. The warning about a small price adds the other half, that recognition can be overridden by interest.

crossReferences.why: States the same relationship, a book sent down confirming what was between its hands already.
Calls the revelation both confirming of earlier scripture and a guardian watching over it.
Has Jesus describe himself as confirming the Torah, the same relation in an earlier link of the chain.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you know to be right and have quietly declined to say, because saying it would cost you standing with a particular group. Name the price to yourself in plain terms today. You do not have to act on it yet. Pricing it accurately is the step most people skip, and it is the step this ayah is about.

studies.title: Reading It And Forgetting Yourself
studies.meaning: The Arabic for mixing truth with falsehood is actually a verb for dressing, so the picture is a disguise rather than a dilution: truth put into borrowed clothing until nobody can identify it. Concealment is named beside it, with the aggravating clause attached, that they know. Three practices are then named, the third of them shared rather than private. The closing question is the famous one, and commentators are careful about it. It faults forgetting oneself, not the instructing.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's address to those who already possessed scripture and the learning that went with it. Medina's older communities included men whose authority rested on reading and explaining texts, and the passage speaks to that position. Classical commentators read the last of these ayat as directed at scholars in particular, and they add that abandoning the teaching would double the fault rather than remove it.

keyTerms.note: From the root that gives the ordinary word for a garment. The instruction is not about blending two substances but about putting the wrong covering on something so that it passes for what it is not.
A wide word for goodness done to others, used in the Quran of kindness to parents and of righteousness generally. It names a whole disposition rather than a particular act.

Ordinary forgetting, and also deliberate setting aside. The choice is exact, since the failing described is not hypocrisy in the sense of pretending but of genuinely leaving oneself out of the account.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Cloth announced who you were. A man's dress marked his tribe, his means and often his trade, and disguise was a known device: an unrecognised figure at night was simply someone wearing a cloak that was not his. Traders also knew the practice of dressing poor goods in good wrapping. An audience hearing about truth being clothed in falsehood would have seen the operation, not a metaphor.
studies.didYouKnow: Nearly the same sentence appears again later in the Quran, in another surah, addressed to the same audience and using the same verb for clothing truth in falsehood. The repetition across two surahs is close enough that commentators regularly treat the two passages together and explain them with the same examples.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates two failures that usually get merged. Concealing is one thing; disguising is another and worse, because it leaves something in circulation that looks like the truth. The closing question then turns the whole reproach inward and makes reading the text a form of exposure rather than of safety. Knowledge is presented here as raising the standard a person is measured against, never as satisfying it.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the charge almost word for word, clothing truth with falsehood while knowing what is being done.
States the same reproach in general terms, asking why people say what they do not do.
Returns later in this surah to those who conceal what was sent down after it was made clear.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you have said recently that was technically accurate and designed to leave a false impression. Everybody has one. You do not need to correct it publicly. Just identify it, name what the true version would have sounded like, and notice how small the distance between them was.

studies.title: Two Resources For Hard Days
studies.meaning: Two things are named as sources of help, and both are demanding: holding steady, and prayer. The passage then admits the difficulty rather than talking past it, saying the practice is heavy except for those who bow. What makes it lighter is described in the next line as an expectation, that they will meet their Lord and return to Him. So the difficulty is not removed by willpower but by a change in what the person believes the effort is for.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a long section addressed to the Children of Israel, recalling favours received and commitments made. The address here widens enough that the classical commentators read the counsel as general, then narrows again in the third line. The surrounding ayat rebuke those who preach to others while neglecting themselves, which places this advice pointedly: seek the help you have been recommending.

keyTerms.note: Wider than patience in English. The root is used for binding something in place and for a bitter medicinal plant, so it carries holding fast and swallowing something hard together.
Used for ground that has sunk down and for a voice that drops. It describes a lowering that is inward before it is postural, the state in which the weight described stops being felt as weight.

keyTerms.gloss: they expect, they hold as certain
keyTerms.note: Ordinarily this verb means to think or suppose, but the commentators read it here as settled expectation. The same word can slide between guessing and knowing, and context decides which.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Both practices had a physical cost in that setting. The prayer interrupted trade and travel five times, and a merchant halting at midday in a market stopped earning while others did not. Endurance was the desert virtue everyone already respected, praised in poetry as the mark of a man who kept his word under pressure. Naming the two together took a familiar tribal ideal and attached it to something that cost time in public.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of steadfastness and prayer appears twice in this surah within a hundred ayat, at this point and again later in almost identical words, but the second time the address narrows to those who believe and adds that God is with the steadfast. The classical commentators treat the repetition as deliberate, the second use answering the difficulty admitted in the first.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Help is offered as a practice rather than a rescue, which sets the tone for how the Quran treats hardship generally. The one thing said to make the practice bearable is a conviction about where a life is heading, so belief about the end reshapes the experience of the middle. And by admitting that the counsel is heavy, the passage refuses to pretend that faith removes strain rather than redirecting it.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same counsel to believers and adds the promise that God is with the steadfast.
Instructs the Prophet to keep his household in prayer and to be patient with it himself.
Contrasts human anxiety under pressure with those steady in prayer, the same diagnosis and remedy.

studies.applyIt: The next time something goes wrong in your day, notice the gap between the news arriving and your first reaction. Put one small thing in that gap: two minutes of stillness, or the next prayer brought slightly forward. You are not trying to feel better. You are practising the order these lines set out, help first and response second, at a scale small enough to keep.

studies.title: Four Exits, All Closed
studies.meaning: Four denials in one sentence, and each names an institution the audience actually used. Nobody discharges another's account, no pleading is accepted from a soul, no compensating equivalent is taken, and no group comes to the rescue. On the third clause, the word usually rendered ransom is a term of balance and exchange. On the second, commentators read the denial alongside passages elsewhere describing pleading that takes place by God's leave, and understand what is refused here as any claim made as of right.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's address to those who possessed earlier scripture, following two ayat that recall a history of favour. Classical commentators note that the ayah is repeated almost exactly later in the same surah, and treat both occurrences as closing off an assumption widespread in that world: that standing, lineage or connection would count for something when the account was finally settled.

keyTerms.note: The verb for settling a debt or standing in for an obligation. It names the specific act of one party covering what another owes, which is exactly what is being ruled out.
From a root meaning even or paired. The one who intercedes joins himself to the one pleaded for, so where there was a single petitioner there are now two. The image is of company, not influence.
From the root for balance and justice. Here it names a compensating weight offered to level a scale, which is why the word for fairness and the word for a payoff are the same word.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every one of these was a working part of Arabian life. A killing was settled by a payment in camels agreed between clans. Captives taken in a raid were released for a price. A weak man in trouble was spoken for by someone stronger, and if all else failed his tribe rode out to help him. A person's security was the sum of these four things. The ayah takes them away one at a time.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah returns later in the same surah with two of its clauses swapped, so that what is refused second here is refused third there. Commentators noticed the switch early and discuss it, and both occurrences fall inside the same long address, which is one reason the pair is usually read together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: By listing four mechanisms rather than making a general statement, the passage establishes that responsibility is not merely undelegated but undelegatable. What can be shared in this life cannot be shared there. That does not present God as unwilling to relent, since the surah says a great deal elsewhere about mercy and pardon. It establishes instead that mercy comes from one direction only, and cannot be arranged sideways between creatures.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same point in family terms, saying no father will discharge anything on behalf of his child.
States it as bare fact, a day on which no soul possesses anything at all for another.
Supplies the other half, describing intercession that occurs only by God's own permission.

studies.applyIt: Notice one thing you are relying on someone else to carry for you: a decision, an apology, an awkward conversation you have quietly handed to a family member. Take the smallest part of it back today and do that part yourself. This ayah is about a limit that already exists, and it is easier to meet it early.

studies.title: Sons Killed, Daughters Spared
studies.meaning: The recollection is deliberately unsoftened. The verb for what was inflicted originally describes driving animals out to pasture, so the persecution is pictured as relentless herding rather than as episodes of cruelty. The policy itself is named exactly: sons killed, women left alive, which is how a people is ended without ending its usefulness. The closing word carries two established senses. Commentators read it as naming the ordeal a trial, or as naming the deliverance a signal favour, and they record both without choosing.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, opening the surah's sequence of recollections addressed to the Children of Israel. Each begins with the same formula, and remember, and each takes up a single episode. This first one goes back before the exodus to the condition the deliverance was from, which classical commentators note is the necessary starting point: the favour cannot be weighed without the state it interrupted.

keyTerms.note: The verb is used of driving livestock out to graze. Applied to people it carries relentlessness and direction, a condition imposed continuously rather than a set of separate cruelties.
Built on the root for life, so the word is literally about letting live. In the same surah a different form of this root carries the sense of shame, which is one root serving two distant meanings.
The word covers testing and also a conspicuous benefit conferred. Commentators divide over which is meant here, and the ambiguity leaves the sentence pointing at both the ordeal and the rescue.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Slavery was ordinary in seventh-century Arabia and its logic was familiar. Captives taken in raids became household labour, status passed to children born into it, and adult men were the security problem while women and children were absorbed into the household. An Arabian audience did not need the policy in this ayah explained. They understood immediately what it was designed to accomplish and how long it would take.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for sparing the women here and the word for feeling shame used earlier in this same surah come from the same three letters. Arabic lexicographers list both senses under one root, connecting them through the idea of holding back: holding back from killing in the one case, holding back out of modesty in the other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Deliverance is presented here as something to be recalled rather than merely believed, and the recollection is made to include the injury. A rescue described without its danger becomes a pleasant fact instead of a debt. The passage also refuses to leave suffering unnamed or spiritualised. What happened is stated in plain words first, and only then is the word for trial placed over it, in an order that keeps the trial from explaining the pain away.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same policy with its motive, describing a ruler who divided the population and weakened one part.
Has Moses himself recall this deliverance to his people in almost identical terms.
Repeats the recollection in another surah, again closing on the word for a great trial.

studies.applyIt: Think of one hard stretch you came out of, and describe it to yourself in the order this ayah uses: the difficulty first, in accurate detail, and only then the way out. Most of us tell it the other way round or skip the first half entirely, and the relief goes thin because there is nothing behind it.

studies.title: A Road Through The Water
studies.meaning: One short ayah holds a rescue and a drowning and puts the same people in front of both. The Arabic construction is unusual: the sea is parted by you or for you, and commentators note the wording, reading the deliverance as happening on their account rather than merely in their vicinity. The closing clause is the point. They were watching. Nothing here was inferred, reported or taken on trust, which is what makes the episodes that follow in this surah so difficult to explain.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, the second in the surah's sequence of recollections. The account is compressed to a single line here while other surahs give it at length with dialogue and pursuit. Classical commentators treat the brevity as deliberate, since the audience knew the story thoroughly; what the surah is doing is not narrating but recalling, item by item, a list of things already granted.

keyTerms.note: The plain verb for dividing one thing into two. Three ayat later the same root names the criterion given to Moses, so a single set of letters covers both the parting of water and the separating of truth from falsehood.
From a root suggesting raising to high ground out of danger. It is the word used across the Quran for prophets brought out of destruction, and it implies extraction rather than escape.
Simple watching, in the present tense, so the clause places them inside the moment rather than remembering it. The grammar makes them witnesses in real time rather than inheritors of an account.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Arabs of the Hijaz were not a seafaring people. The Red Sea was the edge of the world they moved in, and the crossing to Abyssinia, which some of the earliest Muslims made to escape persecution, was a genuine undertaking. Water at that scale was the definitive barrier, the thing that ended a route rather than continuing it. A sea that opens into a road was the image of an exit where there was demonstrably none.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for parting the sea shares its root with the word for the criterion, which appears a few ayat later in this same passage as one of the things given to Moses. The Quran's name for a book that distinguishes true from false is built on the same three letters as an act of physically dividing water.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing rescue and destruction in one sentence keeps them from being two separate lessons. The same event that saved one group ended another, which is how the Quran generally describes deliverance: not as harm avoided but as a division made. The witnessing clause carries the weight for what follows. If seeing were sufficient to settle a person, the rest of this section of the surah would have nothing to report.

crossReferences.why: Tells the crossing at length, including the moment the people believed they had been overtaken.
Gives the instruction to strike out a dry path and describes what then covered the pursuers.
Records what Pharaoh said as the water closed, and the answer he was given.

studies.applyIt: Recall something you personally witnessed that ought to have changed you and did not, or not for long. Not a failure of belief, just of retention. Write one sentence about it and keep the sentence somewhere you will see it. This whole section of the surah turns on how quickly seeing wears off, and noticing your own version is the honest way in.

studies.title: Forty Nights And A Calf
studies.meaning: An absence of forty nights, a substitute made in the meantime, and then a pardon. The verb for that pardon has a striking background. Its root describes wind blowing over tracks in sand until nothing can be followed, so the word does not mean overlooking but erasing. The stated purpose of the pardon is gratitude rather than mere relief. Commentators then differ over the last ayah, reading the Book and the Criterion as two names for one thing or as two distinct gifts.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the surah's recollections. The appointment of forty nights is described in another surah as thirty completed by ten, and classical commentators read the two accounts together rather than as alternatives. The calf episode is given at length elsewhere in the Quran, including the detail that the image was made from ornaments the people were carrying. Here it is compressed to a clause.

keyTerms.note: The period is counted in nights rather than days, which was the ordinary Arabian reckoning. Months began with the sighting of a crescent after sunset, so a span of time was naturally measured from dark to dark.
The root is used of wind wiping out footprints and of a ruin returning to bare ground. Pardon in this word is not a decision to ignore something but the removal of the trace itself.

From the verb for dividing one thing from another. It names whatever draws the line between truth and falsehood, which is why commentators can read it as the scripture itself or as something given alongside it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Tracking was a genuine skill in that world. A man could read from prints in sand who had passed, how many, how heavily loaded and how long ago, and disputes over stolen camels were settled by people who could follow a trail for days. The one thing that defeated them was wind. When the sand had shifted, the trace was not faint but gone, and that is the word this passage uses for pardon.
studies.didYouKnow: The two things given to Moses in the last of these ayat are named with a word for scripture and a word built on the root for splitting. That second root has already appeared in the surah two ayat earlier, describing the parting of the sea, so the same letters carry a physical separation and a moral one within a few lines of each other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The order of events in these three ayat is the argument. Failure comes after an appointment, pardon comes after failure, and the giving of scripture comes after pardon. Nothing is withheld pending improvement. That establishes something about how the relationship is understood to work, and the stated aim of the pardon confirms it: gratitude is presented as the intended result of mercy rather than as its price.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same appointment as thirty nights completed with ten, making the count forty.
Gives the calf episode in full, including the confrontation when Moses returns to find it.
States the consequence for those who made the calf, and what followed for those who turned back afterwards.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you were forgiven that you have kept in your own records anyway, still filed, still consulted. The word used in this passage is about a trace that is genuinely gone. Try, once today, extending that standard to something someone did to you and you have officially let go of but not actually erased.

studies.title: Turn Back To Your Maker
studies.meaning: Moses addresses them as his own people first, then names the wrong exactly and locates the injury in themselves rather than in God. The name he uses for God twice is unusual and pointed: the Originator, the one who brings a thing into being distinct and without flaw, set against an image they had shaped with their hands. The instruction that follows belonged to that community in that moment, and the classical works record more than one account of what it involved and how far it reached. The ayah's own resolution is the turning that God then makes toward them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the surah's recollections. The episode of the calf and its aftermath are told across several surahs, and the accounts of what happened next differ in the classical commentaries, which set the reports side by side rather than harmonising them. What all of them share is the ending given here, that the turning was accepted, and commentators concentrate their comment on the two divine names that close the ayah.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be free of defect and clear of something. It names the maker who brings a thing into existence distinct and whole, which is a pointed choice in a passage about a shaped image.
The verb is simply to return. Repentance in Arabic is not primarily an emotion or a confession but a change of direction, which is why the same word can be used of God turning toward a person.
From the root that also gives the word for a womb. Classical lexicographers connect the two, reading the divine name as naming a mercy that is sustaining and continuous rather than occasional.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Responsibility ran through the group in that society, not around individuals. An offence by one member exposed his whole clan to claim, and clans regularly disciplined their own to prevent a wider reckoning. An instruction addressed to an entire people, requiring the people themselves to act on the matter, fitted a world where a wrong was never merely private and a settlement was never merely personal.
studies.didYouKnow: The name for God used twice in this ayah is rare in the Quran. It appears again in a sequence of divine names near the end of another surah, and almost nowhere else, so a reader working through the text will meet it here in a passage about a manufactured image and then hardly again.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are established by the wording rather than stated. The wrong is described as done to themselves, which locates the damage of turning to a made object in the one who turns rather than in the one turned away from. And the ayah closes with mercy in the strongest form the language has, immediately after its hardest sentence. The tradition reads that placement as the point, since the passage ends where it does deliberately.

crossReferences.why: Places the same rare name for God among the Creator and the Fashioner in a list of divine names.
Records Aaron's warning during the episode and the answer his people gave him.
Describes what followed for those who made the calf and for those who turned back afterwards.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you name your own wrongs to yourself. Most of us describe them by their effect on other people, or by how they looked. This passage names one by what it was and says who it damaged, in that order and without softening. Try writing one sentence about something in that shape, and stop before adding the explanation.

studies.title: Until We See Him Plainly
studies.meaning: The demand is not for evidence but for one particular form of it. The word used means openly, to the eye, in the way an object in front of you is seen, and the condition attached makes belief in the messenger depend on it. What follows is a blast and then a revival, and commentators divide over whether the word for their death is literal or describes a stunning that emptied them of awareness. The second ayah names the purpose of the reversal, and it is the same purpose given for the pardon a few lines earlier.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the sequence of recollections. Another surah connects the demand with a group chosen from among the people to accompany Moses for an appointed meeting, and the classical commentaries read the two passages together. The episode is also recalled elsewhere in almost the same words, which is one reason commentators treat the wording here as fixed rather than as a loose summary.

keyTerms.note: From a root for what is out in the open, used of a voice raised aloud as well as of something visible. It specifies a mode of perception, which is what makes the demand a demand about method.

The same word used earlier in this surah for what the people in the storm parable put their fingers in their ears against. It covers both a lightning strike and any blast that empties a person of sense.
The Quran uses this one verb for raising the dead and for dispatching a messenger to a people. Both are a sending out, which is why the language of resurrection and the language of prophecy overlap.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Direct sight was the gold standard of proof in Arabian dispute. A man who had seen a thing himself outranked any number who had heard about it, and testimony in an assembly was weighed by how close the witness had stood. Applying that standard was not obtuse; it was correct procedure everywhere else in their lives. The passage does not fault them for wanting evidence. It answers a demand for the wrong kind.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for reviving them is the one the Quran uses for raising the dead on the last day and also for sending a prophet to a community. Arabic makes no distinction between the two dispatches, so a reader meets the same word describing a messenger being sent and a body being brought back.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Whether and how God may be seen has been discussed at great length in the tradition, and the discussion is not settled here. What this passage does establish is narrower and firmer: making belief conditional on a chosen form of proof puts the condition where it does not belong. The rest of the sentence answers that on its own terms, since the reversal of death that follows was itself witnessed and still did not function as the guarantee they had asked for.

crossReferences.why: Recalls the same demand in nearly identical words, calling it a request for something greater still.
Records Moses asking to see, and what happened to the mountain when it was shown.
Names the group chosen for the appointed meeting and describes what overtook them.

studies.applyIt: Identify one condition you have quietly attached to trusting something: a sign you are waiting for, a proof you have decided would settle it. Say it out loud in full, as a sentence beginning with the word until. Hearing your own condition stated completely is usually enough to show you what you have actually been doing.

studies.title: Cloud, Manna And Quail
studies.meaning: Three provisions arrive without labour: shade that travels with them, and food of two kinds sent down. Commentators differ over what exactly the first food was, some describing a sweet substance found in the morning, others treating the word as a general term for whatever came as a gift rather than as a crop. Then the sentence turns. Halfway through, the address changes from you to they, so that the naming of the wrong is spoken about them rather than to them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the surah's recollections of what was given during the years in the wilderness. Another surah pairs the same two foods with the twelve springs and the tribal divisions, and classical commentators assemble the accounts into a single period rather than treating them as separate incidents. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah, which belongs to the sequence rather than to an event.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to cover over. The same three letters give the ordinary Arabic word for grief, understood by lexicographers as what covers the heart, so covering is the shared idea.
Shares a root with the words for a favour bestowed and for reminding someone of a favour given. Commentators split between a particular substance and a general term for what arrives unearned.
The plural of a word meaning pleasant, clean and agreeable. It describes food by its quality rather than by its category, and the same root is used of good speech and good land.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Shade was the scarce commodity, more than food. A day's travel was planned around where cover would be at midday, and a single acacia or a rock overhang on a route was known by name and argued over. Caravans halted through the worst hours and moved at the edges of the day. To describe a cloud that stayed above a moving people was to describe something more extravagant to that audience than any meal.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah begins by addressing the audience directly and ends by speaking about them in the third person. The switch happens in the middle of a sentence, at exactly the point where the wrong is named. Arabic rhetoricians have a term for this kind of pivot and treat it as a deliberate device, and commentators note this ayah as an instance of it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The closing clause corrects a natural assumption about what is at stake when a gift is treated badly. Nothing is added to God by gratitude and nothing taken from Him by its absence, so the damage of ingratitude falls entirely on the one who is ungrateful. That makes thankfulness a matter of accuracy rather than of politeness. The passage also presents provision arriving before it is deserved, which is the pattern this whole section keeps repeating.

crossReferences.why: Pairs the same two foods with the springs given for the tribes, in a fuller telling.
Repeats the provision with a warning attached about going too far in what has been given.
Puts the same instruction generally, to eat of good provision and be thankful for the favour.

studies.applyIt: Eat one meal today that you did not choose, cook or pay for, if such a meal comes your way, and say something specific about it to whoever provided it. If no such meal appears, name the last one that did. The passage is about noticing provision that arrives without your arrangement, and most of it goes past unremarked.

studies.title: One Word At The Gate
studies.meaning: Entry, food without limit, and two conditions attached to the manner of arriving rather than to anything else. The word they were given to say is remarkable. It comes from the verb for lifting a load down off a camel's back at the end of a stage, so what they were asked to pronounce was a request to be unburdened. Commentators do not name the town, and neither does the Quran; they record several suggestions and leave it. The final clause adds something not asked for, an increase for those who do well.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the recollections. The episode appears again in another surah in nearly the same words, and classical commentators read the two together. They differ on the identity of the settlement and on whether the instruction about the gate describes a posture or an attitude, generally settling on lowered bearing rather than any particular physical form, and they do not press beyond what the text says.

keyTerms.note: A single word from the verb for setting a load on the ground. Given as something to say, it makes the request itself the act: asking that a weight be taken off rather than describing one.
A plural form describing how they were to enter. Commentators read it as lowered bearing rather than a specific posture, since the instruction concerns the manner of arriving at a place.
From a root meaning both good and beautiful. It names doing a thing well beyond what was asked, which is why the increase promised to them is placed outside the terms already stated.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: At the end of a day's march the camels were couched and the loads lifted off, and the word for that unloading is the word this passage puts in their mouths. Anyone who had travelled with goods knew the specific relief of that moment, when the animals stopped shifting and the weight was on the ground. It is the plainest possible image for asking that something be taken off you.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about eating plentifully wherever you wish appears in this surah once before, in the instruction given to the first human being in the Garden. The same wording is used at the gate of a town, so a reader working through the surah meets an unmistakable echo, with a spoken word required in the second case where a tree was withheld in the first.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What is asked at the gate costs nothing material. The conditions are a bearing and a single word, and against them stand an open town and unlimited provision. That ratio makes the terms of pardon a matter of posture rather than of payment, which is consistent with how the surah has described forgiveness elsewhere. The addition at the end goes further, promising increase to those who do well, so the arrangement is not merely a settling of accounts.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same instruction about the gate and the word, in nearly identical wording.
Uses the same phrase about eating plentifully wherever you wish, in the Garden rather than at a gate.
Recalls the covenant and the instruction to enter the gate bowing, among other undertakings.

studies.applyIt: Find the shortest true sentence for something you have been carrying and say it once, out loud, when nobody is in the room. Not an explanation and not a full account. One short line. The passage puts a single word at the gate, and there is something in the brevity that longer versions of the same thing keep losing.

studies.title: A Different Word Entirely
studies.meaning: One word was given and another was said in its place. That is the whole of the offence, and the Arabic keeps it precise: a saying other than the one that was said to them. Notice what the sentence does next. Instead of using a pronoun the second time, it repeats the phrase for those who did wrong, so the consequence is attached to that group again by name. Commentators point out that this repetition narrows the scope rather than widening it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following directly on the instruction at the gate. The same pair of ayat appears in another surah, again with the substitution named and the consequence following. Classical commentators report various accounts of what was said instead and of what the scourge consisted of, and they are cautious here, generally noting that the Quran specifies neither and declining to fill in more than the text does.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb meaning to put one thing in the place of another. It is not about mishearing or forgetting. The word describes a swap made, which requires knowing what was there to begin with.
Indefinite in the Arabic, so the offence is not a specific alternative formula but any saying that was not the one given. The vagueness is the point, since only one thing had been asked for.
A word used in the Quran for various visitations sent upon a people. Commentators pass on several accounts of what it was here and generally leave the question where the text leaves it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a mostly unwritten society, exactness in transmission was a trained skill and a serious responsibility. Messages between clans were carried by men chosen for accurate memory, poems were passed on line by line, and genealogies were recited without variation. Everybody also knew the person who improved a message in the retelling. Changing a word entrusted to you was a recognised failure with consequences that people could name.
studies.didYouKnow: Arabic would ordinarily use a pronoun for the second mention of a group already named in the same sentence. This ayah does not, repeating the full phrase instead. Commentators from early on treat the repetition as deliberate and read it as confining the consequence strictly to those who made the substitution, rather than to everyone who was present at the gate.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats a word as a thing that can be held in trust, which makes accuracy in transmission a moral matter and not merely a technical one. What was asked for at the gate cost nothing, so the substitution cannot be explained by difficulty. That leaves it as a small act of reassertion, changing what you were given in order to remain the author of it, and the surah locates a great deal of trouble in exactly that impulse.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same substitution and consequence in another surah, in almost identical wording.
Describes words being displaced from their proper places, and speech twisted with the tongue.
Speaks of hearts hardening and words being moved from their positions after a covenant was broken.

studies.applyIt: Repeat one thing today exactly as it was said to you, rather than in your own words. A message from one person to another, an instruction, a piece of news. Notice how strong the pull is to adjust it slightly, and let the adjustment go unmade. The pull is the thing worth observing here.

studies.title: Twelve Springs From One Rock
studies.meaning: Moses asks for water on behalf of others, and the Arabic form of the verb carries exactly that, seeking something for someone else. What comes is more specific than what was asked for. Not water, but twelve outlets, one for each group, so that every party knew where to drink without dispute. Commentators note that a different verb is used in the parallel account elsewhere, a gentler word for water welling up, and they read the two as describing different moments of the same event.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the recollections of the wilderness years. The tribal division into twelve is stated elsewhere in the Quran and assumed here, which is why the number of springs matches without explanation. Classical commentators treat the assignment of a drinking place to each group as the significant detail, since a large camped population sharing one source was the standard occasion for conflict.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb meaning to ask for water, and the construction that follows makes clear he asked on behalf of his people rather than for himself. The request is representative from the start.
A verb of sudden splitting open under pressure. Another surah uses a milder word for the same event, and commentators read the pair as a first welling followed by full flow.
A noun of place from the verb to drink. It names not the water but the spot at which each group drank, which is what the provision actually settled between them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water was the thing people fought over. Wells were owned, inherited and defended, a clan's range was defined by which sources it could reach, and the order in which herds were watered was a standing occasion for dispute. Feuds that lasted generations began at a watering place. Assigning each group its own outlet was not decoration on a miracle. It removed the most reliable cause of bloodshed in that world.
studies.didYouKnow: The parallel account of this event in another surah uses a different verb for the water appearing, one that means to well up gently rather than to burst out. Commentators noticed the difference early and generally read the two words as capturing successive moments, the first seepage and then the full flow, rather than as two versions of one description.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The answer given exceeds the request in a particular direction. What was asked was water; what came was water plus an arrangement that prevented the fight the water would otherwise have caused. That suggests something about how petitions are met, namely that the granting can address a need the petitioner had not named. The closing instruction confirms it, since a provision arriving with a warning about ruin attached assumes the recipients know what they are capable of.

crossReferences.why: Tells the same episode with the tribes named as twelve and a gentler verb for the water.
States the general principle behind this scene, that God is near and answers the one who calls.
Grounds the whole matter, making every living thing from water as a sign for those who deny.

studies.applyIt: Ask for something today on behalf of someone else, by name, without mentioning yourself in it. That is the shape of the request in this ayah and it is a different exercise from praying for yourself. Notice whether you can hold the other person clearly in mind for the length of the asking.

studies.title: Cucumbers, Lentils And Onions
studies.meaning: A complaint about monotony, itemised. The reply turns on one word: would you exchange what is lower for what is better. That word for lower also means nearer at hand, so the sentence names the trade precisely as the immediate against the excellent. Commentators divide on details in this ayah, on whether one of the vegetables is garlic or wheat, and on whether the place named is Egypt specifically or any settled town. The closing clauses attach a consequence to particular acts, which the ayah then names.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the surah's sequence of wilderness recollections. Classical commentators read the closing statements as describing what followed for the generation whose actions are named in the ayah itself, rather than as a permanent description, and they note that the surah goes on almost immediately to say that reward belongs to whoever believes and does good, from whatever community.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning nearness. The word carries both senses at once, so the exchange being questioned is not simply bad for good but the close and available for the genuinely better.
One of the few words in the Quran where the classical lexicographers record two settled readings. Translations still divide between them, and the commentaries pass on both without forcing a choice.
From a root meaning to be brought low or made tractable, used of an animal broken to the yoke. It names a condition of reduced standing rather than an emotion felt about it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The list is farm produce. Cucumbers, lentils and onions grow on irrigated ground that someone tends through a season, and none of it travels with a moving camp. Life away from cultivation meant a narrow diet of dates, milk, bread when grain could be got, and meat occasionally. Families in Arabia moved between settled and nomadic living often enough that this particular longing, for the food of the fields, was entirely familiar.
studies.didYouKnow: One of the vegetables in the list has never been settled. The classical lexicographers record it as garlic and also as wheat, tracing the word to different origins, and English translations still divide between the two readings today. It is a small, honest instance of the commentary tradition preserving a disagreement instead of resolving it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The exchange being questioned is not between something good and something evil, which would be easy to see, but between the better and the merely nearer. That is the harder judgement and the one people get wrong constantly, since availability feels like an argument. The passage also ties its consequence to named actions rather than to identity, which is how the surah handles such statements generally and how the commentaries read this one.

crossReferences.why: Describes a town secure and provided for that denied the favours, and what was then laid on it.
Attaches a warning about going too far to the same wilderness provision described just before.
Follows shortly after in this surah and states that reward turns on belief and action, not on community.

studies.applyIt: Notice one choice today where you take the nearer option over the better one, knowing the difference. The coffee instead of the sleep, the message instead of the call. Do not fix it. Just say the trade out loud in the terms this ayah uses, naming both sides, and see whether you still make it.

studies.title: Reward Measured By Deed
studies.meaning: Four communities are named and then the sentence pivots on a condition: any who believe in God and the Last Day and act righteously. The reward is attached to that condition rather than to the label. Scholars differ sharply over the scope. Many classical commentators read it as describing those who followed their own prophets faithfully before the final message reached them; others read the condition as standing on its own terms. The Quran states the criterion and does not itemise the cases.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside a long address to the Children of Israel recalling deliverance from Pharaoh, the springs in the desert, and repeated breaches of covenant. The passage interrupts that catalogue of failure with a statement of principle. The Sabeans, mentioned only three times in the Quran, were a group the classical commentators already found difficult to identify precisely, and they record several proposals without settling on one.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary commercial word for a worker's pay, not a gift. It implies something earned and owed at the end of a job, which is why the passage attaches it to acting rather than to belonging.
From a root meaning to be in good repair or fit for purpose, the opposite of the word used for corruption. Right action here is work that holds together rather than work that impresses.
Grief over what is already past, distinguished in the same clause from fear, which looks forward. Together they cover the two directions anxiety travels, and both are lifted.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina was religiously mixed in a way Mecca was not. Jewish tribes had been settled there for generations, farming and trading alongside the Arab clans, and Christian merchants and monks were familiar figures on the northern routes. Questions about who stood where before God were not abstract in that town. They came up between neighbours, in-laws and business partners, which is the setting in which this line was heard.
studies.didYouKnow: Nearly the same sentence appears twice more in the Quran, in surahs five and twenty-two, each time with the communities listed in a slightly different order and with small changes in wording. The classical commentators noticed the variation and discussed what each ordering emphasises, which is one of the clearest examples of the Quran restating a principle rather than simply repeating it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The criterion given is conduct joined to belief in God and the coming accounting, and it is stated without reference to community membership. That places the decision about any individual beyond human reach, since no one can audit another's belief or the reach of the message to them. The passage also refuses despair as a settled state for the faithful, promising that neither fear ahead nor grief behind will have the last word.

crossReferences.why: Restates the same principle with the communities listed in a different order.
Names the same groups and says God will decide between them on the Day of Resurrection.
Gives the condition in its shortest form: whoever submits to God and does good.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you place someone in a category and stop thinking about them. It might be a colleague of another faith, or none. Try holding the question of where they stand before God open rather than closed, and let your dealings with them run on what they actually do. That is the discipline this line asks for, and it is easier to hold than to start.

studies.title: Take It With Strength
studies.meaning: A pledge is recalled together with the setting it was made in, a mountain raised above the people who were making it. Two instructions follow and they are not the same. The first concerns grip: take what has been given with strength, a word the commentators gloss as resolve and seriousness rather than physical force. The second concerns retention: remember what is inside it, which they read as continued study rather than a single act of recall. The stated aim is a guarded, mindful life.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the surah's recollections. Another surah describes the mountain raised as though it were a canopy, and classical commentators read the two accounts together. They report differing details of the scene and are restrained about it, concentrating instead on the two verbs, since the same pair of instructions appears elsewhere in the Quran attached to other scriptures and other recipients.

keyTerms.note: The Quran's name for the mountain associated with the revelation to Moses. It is used as a proper name rather than as the ordinary word for a hill, and a whole surah later carries it as a title.
Power, but in the sense of a firm hold and settled determination. Commentators gloss it as taking something seriously and holding to it, not as exerting force on anyone else.
From a root meaning to shield or guard against. The word describes putting something protective between yourself and harm, so the state it names is watchfulness rather than fright.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Agreements in Arabia were tied to places and to physical acts. Parties clasped hands, dipped them together in perfume or blood, and swore at a named landmark that anyone could point to afterwards. The location did the work that a signature does now, because a pledge with no place attached was hard to hold anyone to. A promise made under a mountain held above the crowd is that practice enlarged past all possibility.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction to take the scripture with strength appears more than once in the Quran and not only here. It is given to Moses when the tablets are handed over, and it is given to John as a boy in a single short line. The same two words attach to three different moments of receiving a revealed text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are asked and they answer different failures. A text can be held without being studied, which produces reverence with no content, and it can be studied without being held, which produces information with no grip. Naming both makes the relationship to scripture an active one on two fronts at once. The setting adds a third point, since a pledge made under an overwhelming sign was still, in the event, a pledge that could be turned away from.

crossReferences.why: Describes the mountain raised above them as though it were a canopy, with the same instruction following.
Gives the identical phrase to John as a child, told to take the Book with strength.
Uses the same words when the tablets are handed to Moses, with an instruction to hold to what is best in them.

studies.applyIt: Pick one passage you already believe and read it once as though you were checking what is actually in it, with a pen. Underline anything that surprises you. Holding a text and knowing its contents are separate activities, and most of us do the first much more often than the second.

studies.title: What Kept You From Loss
studies.meaning: The turning away is stated in four words and then interrupted by a clause about favour and mercy, so the sentence never reaches the loss it was heading toward. That structure is the point of the first ayah. What follows recalls a group who broke a boundary and what became of them, and commentators divide over the transformation, most reading it as an outward change and some as a description of what their conduct had already made of them. The last of the three ayat names the purpose: a restraint for others and a counsel.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the surah's recollections. The episode of the boundary broken by a coastal community is told at length in another surah, where the account also records that people among them had spoken against the wrongdoing and were delivered. Classical commentators read the two passages together and note that the Quran itself limits who was affected, both in that fuller telling and in the wording here.

keyTerms.note: The verb for turning your back on someone, from the same root that gives the words for an ally and for turning toward. Direction is the whole of its meaning, which is why it can face either way.
From a root naming a hobble or fetter. A punishment called by this word is defined by its effect on those watching rather than by its severity on those it falls upon.
Advice that works on the heart rather than on the fear, from a root suggesting softening. Placing it beside the harder word gives the episode two audiences and two different effects.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation was preserved in verse. A tribe's disgrace or a famous settlement was composed into poetry and recited at markets and gatherings for generations, so a single episode could restrain behaviour long after everyone involved was dead. Describing something as a deterrent for what came before it and what came after it named a real mechanism in that world, and everyone present knew a story that was still doing that work.
studies.didYouKnow: The fuller account of this episode in another surah records that a group among the same community had objected to the wrongdoing and asked why others bothered warning people who would not listen. That surah states plainly that those who forbade the wrong were delivered, a detail the shorter recollection here leaves out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The first of these ayat establishes something about how consequences are described. A turning away is named, an outcome is named, and between them a clause about mercy prevents the second from following the first. That is the Quran's usual account of why any community continues. The passage also gives a punishment a purpose beyond itself, since a deterrent and a counsel are both directed at people who were not involved.

crossReferences.why: Tells the episode at length, including the objection raised by some and their deliverance.
States the general principle, that immediate reckoning for wrongdoing would leave no creature on earth.
Says the same thing again, that God defers rather than taking people to task for what they earn.

studies.applyIt: Think about something that did not happen to you, a consequence that was available and did not arrive. A near miss, an error nobody noticed, a habit that could have cost far more than it did. Name one, precisely. Gratitude usually attaches to what came, and this passage attaches it to what was withheld.

studies.title: Do You Take Us Lightly
studies.meaning: An instruction is delivered and the response is an accusation of mockery. What Moses says back is the striking part. He seeks refuge from being among the ignorant, and the Arabic word he uses does not mainly mean uninformed. In classical usage it stands opposite forbearance as much as opposite knowledge, naming rashness and the readiness to treat people carelessly. Mockery is therefore not classified here as rudeness but as a defect of restraint, and he distances himself from it rather than defending the instruction.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, opening the episode that gives this surah its name. The narrative is set during the years in the wilderness and is told only here in the Quran, unlike most of the recollections in this section, which appear in other surahs too. Classical commentators note that the surah presents the exchange in dialogue, which is unusual for this stretch of recollections.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for slaughtering an animal, used throughout the Quran without special ceremony attached. Nothing in the word itself signals a rite, which is part of why the instruction seemed so unaccountable to them.
Not the act of mocking but the thing mocked. The accusation is that they are being made into a joke, which is a charge about their standing rather than about the instruction's content.
In classical Arabic this word stands opposite forbearance as much as opposite knowledge. It names unrestrained, headlong conduct, which is why it fits an accusation of mockery so exactly.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Cattle were not the usual wealth of the Arabian interior, where camels and sheep carried a family's value. Cows belonged to settled agriculture, to the irrigated oases and the farming south, where they pulled ploughs and turned the wheels that lifted water. A cow was therefore a working asset with a known price, not a beast anyone kept casually, and an instruction to destroy one had an obvious cost.
studies.didYouKnow: This episode gives the surah its name. The longest chapter of the Quran, running to two hundred and eighty-six ayat and covering law, history, prayer and creed, is called The Cow after an incident that occupies seven of them and is never referred to again. The Quran's surah names are frequently drawn from such incidental details.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The response models something specific. Faced with an accusation, Moses neither argues the point nor asserts his authority. He states what he seeks refuge from, which reframes the exchange as a question about character rather than about who is right. The passage also establishes that an instruction can arrive without its reason attached, and that the absence of a stated reason is not itself grounds for treating it as unserious.

crossReferences.why: Warns against asking about matters which, if made plain, would trouble those asking.
Refers later in this surah to questioning a messenger in the way Moses was questioned before.
Records another ill-judged request made to Moses immediately after the sea was crossed.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you meet an instruction whose reason you have not been given, at work or at home, and watch for the impulse to treat it as unserious. You do not have to comply without thinking. Just separate the question of whether it makes sense from the question of whether you are being taken lightly.

studies.title: Neither Old Nor Young
studies.meaning: The first of three requests for further specification, and the answer narrows the field without explaining anything. Two ages are excluded and a middle range is named, in the vocabulary a livestock buyer would use. Then the reply ends by pointing them back to where they started, telling them to do what they were told. Classical commentators pass on a widely repeated observation about this exchange: that any cow would have satisfied the original instruction, and that each question made the requirement harder to meet.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside the surah's only telling of this episode. The Quran gives the exchange as a sequence of questions and answers rather than as a summary, which is unusual for this stretch of recollections. Commentators treat the escalating specification as the point of the narrative and note that the closing clause of this ayah, returning them to the original instruction, is repeated in effect at each stage.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning the space between two things. To make something clear in Arabic is to separate it from what it might be confused with, which is exactly what they are asking for here.
A specific term for an animal too old to breed. Arabic had precise vocabulary for livestock at every stage, and the words in this ayah come straight from the language of buying and selling.
An animal that has bred once and is in its prime. The word marks a stage rather than a number of years, and it names exactly the range left after the two exclusions.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Livestock ages were graded finely in Arabic and the vocabulary was common property. A camel had a different name at each year of its life, and buyers examined teeth and argued over which stage an animal had reached, because the answer set the price. Anyone hearing this ayah recognised the register immediately. The question had been answered in market language, precisely and without a word of explanation.
studies.didYouKnow: The exchange in this passage is one of the most cited in the whole commentary tradition for a point about questions. Early authorities are quoted as saying that had the people taken any cow at all, it would have counted, and that the specification tightened only because they kept asking. The remark is repeated across the classical works almost as a formula.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage distinguishes between two kinds of asking. Seeking to understand something is not what happens here, since none of the answers give a reason and the questioners never ask for one. What is sought is more specification, which functions to delay. The closing clause treats that as the issue by returning them to the instruction unchanged, which establishes that clarity was never what was missing.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the same habit directly, warning about questions whose answers would prove burdensome.
States the principle that limits any such burden, since no soul is charged beyond its capacity.
Shows the same people making another request that Moses answers by naming their ignorance.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself once today asking for more information about something you already know enough to begin. The extra detail that will not change what you do is the tell. Notice it, and then do the first small part of the thing instead of asking the next question.

studies.title: Yellow, And Bright With It
studies.meaning: The second request asks about colour, and the answer supplies more than a colour. It gives an intensifier, a word Arabic reserves for yellow specifically, and then adds a clause that has nothing to do with identifying an animal at all: she gladdens those who look at her. Nothing in the narrowing so far has been decorative, so the presence of a purely aesthetic detail is worth pausing on. Commentators note the phrase and read it as attributing genuine delight to the sight of a colour.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, the second stage of the specification in the surah's only account of this episode. The narrative is told nowhere else in the Quran, so there is no parallel version to compare the details against. Commentators work from the wording itself, and their comment on this ayah concentrates on the two additions, the intensifier and the clause about the effect on onlookers.

keyTerms.note: The feminine form of the ordinary colour word. Arabic colour terms take this shape, and the same root gives words for a coat turning pale and for the season when leaves change.
An intensifier used only with yellow. Arabic assigns each basic colour its own such word, so a different term would be required for a deep black, a pure white or a strong red.

From the root that gives the word for joy and also for something kept secret. Lexicographers connect them through the idea of what is held inside, since gladness of this kind is felt before it is shown.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Colour was expensive. Bright yellow came from saffron and similar dyes that had to be traded in, and cloth of a strong, even shade signalled means. Herders identified animals by their markings, so a beast of one clean colour with no patches was both unusual and easy to describe. The specification was moving, without saying so, toward an animal that would be very hard to find and costly to buy.
studies.didYouKnow: Arabic keeps a separate intensifying word for each of the main colours, and they are not interchangeable. The one used in this ayah belongs to yellow alone; black, white and red each have their own. The classical dictionaries list these pairings as fixed, so the ayah is using a term that could not appear with any other colour.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A clause about something being pleasant to look at, placed inside a set of technical specifications, treats beauty as a real property of a created thing rather than as a reaction in the viewer. The Quran describes creation this way repeatedly, listing colour and variety among signs alongside function and provision. The detail also complicates the episode, since the animal being described so appealingly is the one about to be slaughtered.

crossReferences.why: Lists streaks of colour in mountains and the varying colours of people and animals among the signs.
Names the variety of human languages and colours as a sign for those who know.
Points to what God has produced on earth in differing colours as a reminder for those who reflect.

studies.applyIt: Find one colour today that you actually enjoy looking at, and look at it for longer than you need to. A wall, a fruit, the sky at a particular hour. This ayah puts pleasure at a colour into a passage that had no other reason to include it, which suggests the noticing is worth doing on purpose.

studies.title: If God Wills, We Will Find It
studies.meaning: The third request repeats the first, word for word, with a reason added: the cows all look alike to them. Then something new appears at the end of the sentence. For the first time in this exchange they attach their intention to God's will, and say that with it they will be guided. Commentators note both the lateness of the qualification and the fact that it works. The answer that follows is the last one, and after it the search ends.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, the third and final stage of the questioning in the surah's only telling of this episode. Classical commentators treat the phrase added at the end of this ayah as the turning point of the whole narrative, since everything up to here had been a request for more detail and this is the first sentence in which the questioners refer the outcome to anyone but themselves.

keyTerms.note: From the root for likeness. The same root appeared earlier in this surah describing the fruit of the Garden brought in resembling forms, where the resemblance was a pleasure rather than a problem.
